title: cocoonery: the story of my first internet home
content:
more on digital ecosystems

I created my first internet home in the summer of 2014, right after graduating college, and in the summer months before starting my 9-5 day job.

before then, I had fragments of myself scattered and abandoned on xangas, myspace, tumblr, and various community-based platforms. I had other tiny websites I made for visual projects. I had an instagram and facebook account, but they felt too exposed, public, and fragmented. I wanted somewhere on the internet where I could wrap myself in my own thoughts without debilitating self-consciousness.

I didn’t start here, with keningzhu.com — I was too young and shy to claim my own domain name. I craved a soft, safe space where I could feel semi-hidden, so I made up a word that was more of a feeling for a place:

cocoonery

  • as in: a place where you go to cocoon (verb).

  • or, a place that makes cocoons (noun).

I built it using a single column wordpress blog template, and named it “cocoonery.co” (because “.com” was not available). the subtitle was “small trails of creativity & curiosity.”

here’s what the earliest version looked like (which I just fished out of wayback machine from internet archives). this was me in July 27, 2014.

a few months later, by autumn of 2015, around when I started my 9-5 job, I would change the visual styling and design to something that felt more like me. I choose a classic serif font and a light pastel blue background, and a minimalist design.

I called cocoonery a “creative daybook,” and featured one of my favorite quotes on the main page:


“Have patience with everything that remains unsolved in your heart. Try to love the questions themselves, like locked rooms and like books written in a foreign language.”

— Rainer Maria Rilke

this quote soothed me — in that it was both instructions to myself, and the guiding ethos of my site. at the time, I was so filled with unanswered questions that I was constantly in a state of existential angst and deep anxiety.

cocoonery was my outlet for circling my way around the questions obliquely; questions like:

what am I supposed to do with my life?
how do I become the artist/writer I want to be?
is this the right relationship for me?
is this the right job for me?
am I always going to feel so restless?
how do I take care of my mental health?
am I doing enough???
how do I know that I’m doing enough???

when I think about cocoonery, I mostly conjure a memory — of me writing on Sunday mornings, for hours, at the corner desk in the bedroom I shared with my then-boyfriend, in our apartment in Washington Heights, Upper Manhattan.

I paired my writings with soft, VSCO-filtered photos I took on my iPhone and meticulously edited — of my houseplants, or the buttermilk pancakes I made, or of snowy scenes from our neighborhood. I spent hours trying to figure out formatting. I felt massive anxiety about posting and sharing my voice. I was constantly blocked, tripping over myself and my suffocating perfectionism. it took me many years to identify and untangle those wires in my head — even now, I still catch myself in them sometimes.

a memory / self-portrait of the creator

when I began writing for cocoonery, I was 22, 23 years old — a recent Columbia graduate with a major in creative nonfiction writing and history, a child immigrant, and the daughter of Chinese engineer immigrants, who were, of course, dismayed at my choice of major and apparent lack of ambition to climb the corporate ladder. the core grounding “elements” of my life — a long-term boyfriend, my little day job — felt like giant lego blocks that were slowly compressing me alive. I could feel that I was on the wrong board game, anchored by the wrong things — but I didn’t know how to get out of it. (those were dark times, which I talk about more in this podcast episode: throwing away the iron rice bowl).

all I knew, for certain, was that I wanted to become a “a writer,” and I attempted to do that — on early mornings before work, and weekends — while during all other hours outside of work and domestic life, I devoured books like “So Good They Can’t Ignore You” by Cal Newport, and “Daily Rituals” by Mason Currey. I was obsessed with productivity (and without even knowing it, a masculine notion of linear productivity) because I felt so alienated from what I wanted. and simultaneously, I felt like an alien in my own life.

the problem was, perhaps, that I didn’t even know how to want what I wanted, not what society or my family told me to want — more money, more status, more prestige. I didn’t realize that I was trapped in the programming of the capitalist, accomplishment-driven identity I’d downloaded by default. I felt an enormous pressure to be a packaged product of optimized, shiny efficiencies; a concrete, responsible money-making machine my parents could be proud of.

of course, that never happened.

somewhere, deep down, maybe, I sensed that I longed for something more — something messier and more chaotic, more liberated and formless, more beautiful and monsterous, more possible. I wanted a process and practice that was truly mine; not a product blueprint that was handed down to me.

(I talk about this more here: the process is the way)

a place to ask myself things & answer them

cocoonery was the first place where I processed things outloud, in “public,” — where I wrote to articulate my ideas around what I was obsessed with those days (wellbeing, productivity, and creativity). and if I was embarrassed that it read as a bit “self-help-y,” that’s because I was literally trying to help myself, by writing instructions-to-self that could center me as I wandered through the world, overwhelmed, overstimulated, and so porous I easily forgot who I was.

here’s the index that I accumulated over those years:

I wrote at a pace of less than 1 post per month, but each post, back then, took an enormous amount of energy (and wading through the friction of perfectionism).

here’s a list of ideas and unpublished notes from that period.

migration to my current website

I wrote on cocoonery.co from July 2014 (right after graduating college) until April 2016 (a few months after quitting my first and only 9-5 job).

sometime in late 2015, while working a full time job, taking continuing ed design classes at School of Visual Arts, and stumbling through my first client projects, I built my personal website — keningzhu.com — on Squarespace. I used my website as a portfolio space for graphic and visual work, and as a services landing page for clients to hire me. my first iteration of this website was very much “website as brochure,” (albeit an aesthetic one), because I didn’t know how else to do it.

by spring of 2016, I felt like I couldn’t handle having two websites — so I decided that I wanted to concentrate all of my work on one space. I migrated a very small selection of posts from cocoonery to keningzhu.com, and then I eventually deleted cocoonery. here’s a few old posts I migrated, in case you’re curious.

(please note: I may or may not agree with anything that I wrote over 10 years ago!)

magic hour: how to build a daily creative ritual
everything I know about starting a morning routine
creatives vs. creative professionals

a cocoon is a tender membrane around process

for the last eight years, I’ve barely thought about cocoonery.

then, last autumn, while re-birthing my house on the webs course, I made an entire module around around idea of the website as cocoon. it was then that I remembered that I actually had a first web cocoon, before this one, literally called cocoonery.

at 22, I choose the word “cocoonery” without really understanding why. now, it feels self-evident in a deeply poetic way. cocoonery was my way of making a psychic space for the parts of me that desperately wanted to explore, expand, and change, but didn’t know in exactly which way, or how. I did it slowly. word by word, piece by piece. I did it by sharing my process in a container I created, and allowing myself a semi-permeable veil through which I could be seen.

a cocoon is a tender membrane around process.
a cocoon is a container for change.

recently, I’ve been noticing how my work is shaped by the reoccuring metaphors of worlds, labyrinths, and cocoons. at the time of writing this, I have 658 posts in my journal, from over 10 years of wayfinding through writing. I’ve never claimed to have anything “figured out;” I can only write as an act of breathing, thinking, metabolizing out loud. my website world has become an archive of all the lives I’ve lived, and messy, in-process ways in which I’ve allowed myself to be, always, in a state of change.

the greatest gift that cocoonery gave to me — which this website continued on — is a deep, embodied connection to personal processes and practices. this was — and continues to be — exactly what I needed.
